# Numerical methods {#sec-methods}

This chapter fixes the notation and the two time-stepping strategies used
throughout. Individual application chapters refer back to it rather than
restating it.

## Reciprocal-space convention {#sec-klap}

Every spectral application is written in terms of the **Laplacian symbol**

$$
u \;=\; k_{\mathrm{lap}} \;=\; -|\mathbf{k}|^2 ,
$$ {#eq-klap}

so that $\widehat{\nabla^2 \psi} = u\,\hat\psi$ exactly. Using $u$ rather than
$|\mathbf{k}|$ keeps every operator a *polynomial with no square roots*:
$\nabla^4 \mapsto u^2$, $\nabla^6 \mapsto u^3$. It also makes the sign
bookkeeping uniform — $u$ is negative for every mode except $\mathbf{k}=0$,
which is where conservation lives.

A conserved equation is one whose evolution operator carries an explicit factor
of $u$. Because $u=0$ at $\mathbf{k}=0$, the mean of the field is then
annihilated *exactly*, not to within a tolerance — a property several
application chapters assert bit-exactly rather than numerically.

## Spectral exponential time differencing {#sec-etd}

The spectral applications share one semi-discrete form. Splitting the right
hand side into a part linear in the unknown and a remainder,

$$
\partial_t \hat\psi(\mathbf{k},t)
  = L(k)\,\hat\psi(\mathbf{k},t)
  + M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k)\,\widehat{N[\psi]}(\mathbf{k},t),
$$ {#eq-etd-semi}

where $L$ and $M_{\mathrm{nl}}$ are pointwise multipliers and $N$ is evaluated
in real space. Integrating the linear part exactly over one step gives the
first-order exponential time differencing (ETD1) update

$$
\hat\psi^{\,n+1}
  = e^{L\Delta t}\,\hat\psi^{\,n}
  + \frac{e^{L\Delta t}-1}{L}\,M_{\mathrm{nl}}\,\widehat{N[\psi^{\,n}]},
$$ {#eq-etd1}

with the coefficient evaluated by its Taylor series where $|L\Delta t|$ is
small enough for the quotient to lose precision.

The point of @eq-etd1 is that **all of the stiffness sits inside
$e^{L\Delta t}$**, which is a pointwise multiply and is unconditionally stable
for $L<0$ no matter how negative $L$ becomes. A $k^{10}$ operator is no less
stable than a $k^2$ one. The timestep is then limited by the *nonlinearity* and
by accuracy, not by the highest derivative in the equation.

The practical size of that effect is worth stating concretely. On a grid with
$\Delta x = 2\pi/8$ the Nyquist wave number is $k_{\max}=4$, and a sixth-order
operator with unit coefficient has $|L(k_{\max})| \approx 4^6 = 4096$, so
forward Euler would need $\Delta t < 2/|L| \approx 5\times 10^{-4}$. The
corresponding tenth-order operator needs $\Delta t \lesssim 2\times 10^{-6}$.
ETD runs both at the timestep the physics wants.

One step therefore costs two transforms — a forward transform of $N$ and an
inverse transform of the updated field — plus $O(1)$ work per mode.

### Dealiasing

Where $N$ is polynomial, the product raises the highest wave number present:
$\psi^2$ doubles it and $\psi^3$ triples it. On a finite grid that content
folds back onto resolved modes. Applications with a polynomial nonlinearity
therefore apply the Orszag 2/3 rule, zeroing the upper third of the spectrum
after each nonlinear evaluation. Purely linear applications
(@sec-surface-diffusion) do not need it and switch it off.

## Finite differences {#sec-fd-methods}

The finite-difference applications discretise derivatives with centred
stencils of even order $2m$, exchanging $m$ ghost cells per face before each
evaluation. OpenPFC provides the halo exchange for host and device fields,
including a GPU-aware path that passes device pointers to MPI directly when
the installation supports it.

Time stepping is explicit — forward Euler, or a Runge–Kutta scheme where the
application needs it — and therefore subject to the usual parabolic condition

$$
\Delta t \;\lesssim\; \frac{\Delta x^2}{2 d\, D}
$$ {#eq-cfl}

in $d$ dimensions for a diffusion coefficient $D$. This is exactly the
constraint ETD removes for the spectral applications, and it is why the
finite-difference applications in this report are second-order-in-space
problems rather than sixth.

## What "verified" means here

Each application chapter ends with a *Verification* section. The tests behind
those sections fall into four kinds, and it is worth distinguishing them:

* **Analytical** — the discrete operator is compared against a closed-form
  symbol or solution, typically to $10^{-12}$ or better. This is the strongest
  kind and most of the spectral applications have one, because a single
  Fourier mode of a linear operator has an exact answer.
* **Conservation** — a quantity the formulation should preserve is checked,
  in several cases bit-exactly.
* **Convergence** — the error is measured against a refined or analytic
  solution across resolutions and the observed order compared to the design
  order.
* **Regression** — a checksum is pinned so that a change of decomposition,
  backend, or platform is detected. These catch ports, not physics.

Where an application has only regression coverage for some property, the
chapter says so.
